questions.article: Carrying on the Legacy and Mission of Maulana
questions.q: Before his death, Maulana Wahiduddin Khan recorded a message on how his students should respond to the news of his passing. What were they to say?
options: “Maulana is no more, but God is still alive!”
Yes. As Abu Bakr said at the Prophet’s death – God alone is eternal.
“Let us wait for another guide”
Not quite. The article says: “Maulana is no more, but God is still alive!”.
“Who will lead us now?”
Not quite. The article says: “Maulana is no more, but God is still alive!”.
“The mission has ended with him”
Not quite. The article says: “Maulana is no more, but God is still alive!”.
questions.rationale: “If tomorrow you receive the news, Maulana is no more, what should be your reaction? You should immediately exclaim, Maulana is no more, but God is still alive!”

questions.q: When Zakaria saw the spiritual provision granted to Mary and asked where it came from, what did she reply?
options: “I do not know”
Not quite. The article says: “This is from God”.
“This is from God”
Right. Such inner states are a gift, not of one’s own making.
“This is from my family”
Not quite. The article says: “This is from God”.
“This is from my own effort alone”
Not quite. The article says: “This is from God”.
questions.rationale: “‘Mary, where did this provision come from?’ She replied, ‘This is from God.’ (3: 37)”

questions.q: The Prophet met the severest hardships yet achieved great success. Which Quranic assurance does the article connect with this?
options: “Man was created impatient”
Not quite. The article says: “Surely with every hardship there is ease” (94:5).
“Every soul shall taste death”
Not quite. The article says: “Surely with every hardship there is ease” (94:5).
“Wealth and children are a trial”
Not quite. The article says: “Surely with every hardship there is ease” (94:5).
“Surely with every hardship there is ease” (94:5)
Well read. So there is no ground for despair.
questions.rationale: “This is what the Quran means by saying that ‘Surely with every hardship there is ease.’ (94: 5)”

questions.q: When people work together, credit is never shared evenly. What does the article call the only way for a common effort to prosper?
options: For credit to be decided by vote
Not quite. The article says: For people to forget their rights and remember their responsibilities.
For people to forget their rights and remember their responsibilities
Yes. The work itself is reward enough.
For every reward to be divided equally
Not quite. The article says: For people to forget their rights and remember their responsibilities.
For one person to do all the work
Not quite. The article says: For people to forget their rights and remember their responsibilities.
questions.rationale: “There is only one way for a common effort to prosper, and that is for people to forget about their rights, and remember only their responsibilities.”

questions.q: A Persian couplet says two people hear the same door differently. How?
options: One hears it lock; the other hears it break
Not quite. The article says: One hears it being shut; the other hears it being opened.
One hears a knock; the other hears a voice
Not quite. The article says: One hears it being shut; the other hears it being opened.
One hears it creak; the other hears nothing
Not quite. The article says: One hears it being shut; the other hears it being opened.
One hears it being shut; the other hears it being opened
Right. The difference lies in the mind.
questions.rationale: “You hear the sound of a door being shut, while I hear the sound of a door being opened.”

questions.q: What does the article call the “in spite of” principle?
options: Refusing to deal with difficult people
Not quite. The article says: Staying positive and moving ahead despite opposition and unpleasantness, since these will always be there.
Giving up when conditions are unfavourable
Not quite. The article says: Staying positive and moving ahead despite opposition and unpleasantness, since these will always be there.
Complaining until matters improve
Not quite. The article says: Staying positive and moving ahead despite opposition and unpleasantness, since these will always be there.
Staying positive and moving ahead despite opposition and unpleasantness, since these will always be there
Well reasoned. Reaching the flowers despite the thorns.
questions.rationale: “In spite of all opposition, he must attempt to incline people in his favour; in spite of there being a great deal of unpleasantness in this life, he must learn the secret of harmonious living.”

questions.q: How did the Prophet Yusuf explain the king’s dream of the cows and the ears of corn?
options: Seven years of good harvests would be followed by seven years of drought
Yes. So the plenty had to be stored.
Seven enemies would attack the kingdom
Not quite. The article says: Seven years of good harvests would be followed by seven years of drought.
Seven sons would be born to the king
Not quite. The article says: Seven years of good harvests would be followed by seven years of drought.
Seven rivers would flood the land
Not quite. The article says: Seven years of good harvests would be followed by seven years of drought.
questions.rationale: “Seven fat cows means seven years of good harvests. After the first seven years, there’ll be seven more years of drought.”

questions.q: Made minister, what did Yusuf do that kept the kingdom safe when the drought came?
options: He had the surplus grain of the good years saved and stored
Correct. Wisdom joined with foresight.
He dug canals to the sea
Not quite. The article says: He had the surplus grain of the good years saved and stored.
He bought grain from other lands
Not quite. The article says: He had the surplus grain of the good years saved and stored.
He moved the people elsewhere
Not quite. The article says: He had the surplus grain of the good years saved and stored.
questions.rationale: “The new minister made sure that the extra wheat was saved and stored. When the water dried up and the drought finally came, the kingdom was safe once more.”

questions.q: Marching with his army, the Prophet Sulayman heard an ant warn the others. What did he do?
options: He ignored the ants
Not quite. The article says: He smiled, halted his army so the ants could reach safety, and thanked God for His gifts.
He smiled, halted his army so the ants could reach safety, and thanked God for His gifts
Exactly. Power used with care for the smallest creature.
He took another road without stopping
Not quite. The article says: He smiled, halted his army so the ants could reach safety, and thanked God for His gifts.
He ordered the army to march faster
Not quite. The article says: He smiled, halted his army so the ants could reach safety, and thanked God for His gifts.
questions.rationale: “He stopped his army so the ants could scatter to safety… Then the Prophet Sulayman thanked Allah for the gifts that He had given him.”

questions.q: “Man is born impatient: when misfortune touches him he laments, and when good fortune comes he grows niggardly.” Whom do the verses (70:19-35) except from this?
options: Those who are born wealthy
Not quite. The article says: Those steadfast in prayer, who share their wealth with the needy and are faithful to their trusts and pledges.
Those who live far from others
Not quite. The article says: Those steadfast in prayer, who share their wealth with the needy and are faithful to their trusts and pledges.
Those who never face misfortune
Not quite. The article says: Those steadfast in prayer, who share their wealth with the needy and are faithful to their trusts and pledges.
Those steadfast in prayer, who share their wealth with the needy and are faithful to their trusts and pledges
Well read. Faith steadies both grief and plenty.
questions.rationale: “But not so the worshippers who are steadfast in prayer; those who give a due share of their wealth to those who ask [for help] and to the destitute… and those who are faithful to their trusts and to their pledges.”
